questions.q: What is the first step in this lesson's four-step iteration loop?
options: Baseline — run the current prompt against a fixed set of test inputs and save the outputs
Immediately rewrite the entire prompt from scratch
Delete all previous versions of the prompt
Change the output format before anything else
questions.explain: Establishing a baseline first gives you something concrete to compare future changes against.

questions.q: Why does this lesson recommend changing only one thing per iteration?
options: Because models can only process one instruction per prompt
So that any improvement or regression can be attributed to a specific, known change
Because multiple changes always make a prompt longer than the token limit
It doesn't matter — any number of simultaneous changes works equally well
questions.explain: Changing one variable at a time means you know exactly which edit caused a result, good or bad, instead of guessing among several changes.

questions.q: In the worked ticket-classifier example, what was the recommended fix for tickets mentioning both billing and a bug?
options: Rewrite the entire prompt from scratch
Add one sentence resolving the specific ambiguity, then re-run the full test set
Lower the classifier's required accuracy threshold
Remove billing as a valid category entirely
questions.explain: The lesson's recommended move was a targeted, single addition addressing the specific ambiguity, followed by a full re-run to check for regressions.

questions.q: What is a "regression" in the context of this lesson's iteration loop?
options: A prompt that produces output in the wrong language
A test case that was already failing before any changes were made
A previously-working case that breaks because of a change made for a different case
A prompt that takes longer than expected to run
questions.explain: A regression is when fixing one issue accidentally breaks a case that used to work — which is exactly what re-running the full test set is meant to catch.

questions.q: Why does this lesson say re-running the FULL test set matters, not just the specific cases you were trying to fix?
options: It's required by the model provider's terms of service
It makes the prompt shorter overall
It catches regressions — cases that worked before but broke because of the new change
It has no real benefit; testing only the fixed cases is equally reliable
questions.explain: Only checking the cases you were fixing would miss any previously-working case that the change accidentally broke.
